report:
## Conclusion

Your skepticism is well-supported: the claim that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 is **not backed by solid evidence** and is now considered largely debunked.

## What happened and what the evidence shows

The scare originated in March 2020 when French Health Minister Olivier Véran warned against NSAIDs based on a *Lancet* letter hypothesizing that anti-inflammatories could upregulate ACE2 receptors—the entry point SARS-CoV-2 uses to infect cells—potentially worsening infection ([sciencealert.com](https://www.sciencealert.com/who-recommends-to-avoid-taking-ibuprofen-for-covid-19-symptoms); [nbcnews.com](https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/should-you-be-worried-about-taking-ibuprofen-coronavirus-no-experts-n1162816)). This was a theoretical mechanism, not a clinical finding.

The WHO initially echoed caution but quickly reversed course, stating there was **no evidence** ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 outcomes ([cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496)). Subsequent clinical research has consistently failed to confirm harm. A 38,000-patient study found NSAID use was **not associated with increased COVID-19 severity**, mortality, ventilation, or kidney injury—and one analysis even found *decreased* severity and mortality among NSAID users ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9107579/)). A systematic review similarly concluded NSAID exposure did not increase infection risk or disease severity, though it noted study quality limitations ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8426976/)).

## Bottom line

The ibuprofen-worsens-COVID-19 claim originated from an unproven biological hypothesis, not observed clinical harm. Major health bodies retracted early cautionary advice, and accumulated observational data—while not flawless—consistently show no increased risk, and some suggest possible benefit. The claim is best characterized as false or at minimum unsupported by evidence.
